backTranslations.41: **Before your visit** - In the Visit tab, add the appointment date. MenoMap shows how far along your notes are and what you could add to make them more useful. Choose the most important topics and questions; narrow them to three or four. Create notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check whether your medication list is up to date. **At the visit** - Hand over page 1 or show it on screen. It is designed to be readable in under a minute; it contains counts, averages, a hot flash calendar, and your questions. Start with the question most important to you. If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language. **What the notes can and cannot tell you** - The notes are a summary of what you entered plus information you chose to import from Health. They are not a diagnosis, nor a complete medical record. The trends shown in the notes are for checking coincidence and are not proof of a cause. Doctors may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal. **After the visit** - If there is a new medication, add it with its start date. After a few weeks MenoMap can show your records from before and after starting, making the next review easier.
backTranslations.42: **Menopause** refers to a single point in time: the day that marks 12 months of no periods that cannot be explained by other reasons such as pregnancy, certain medications, or surgery. In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but it is common for it to happen anywhere from the mid-40s to the mid-50s. **The time leading up to menopause** (menopausal transition) is the several years up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall irregularly, so periods become irregular, heavier or lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin in this period when you still have periods. This period may end in a few years or may last quite long, and how it shows up differs by person. **Post-menopause** is the whole time after that 12-month mark. Some symptoms settle over time, others continue for years. Surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments and other health conditions can also cause menopause to happen earlier. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and is worth discussing with a doctor. **How it is determined.** For many people 45 or older, doctors judge from the course and symptoms whether you are approaching menopause or have reached it. Hormone levels vary greatly from day to day, so blood tests are not always necessary. Blood tests are more likely to be used when the person is younger or the situation is unclear. **What MenoMap can and cannot do.** MenoMap cannot tell which stage you are in now. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice, such as hot flashes, sleep, mood, and treatment. Then you and your doctor can look at the same overall picture.

backTranslations.162: In medical settings, hot flashes and night sweats are called **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sensation like a wave of heat suddenly rushing over the face, neck, chest and so on; it may come with facial redness, sweating, and palpitations, and may be followed by chills. Night sweats are the same phenomenon during sleep, and can be strong enough to wake you or soak the sheets. Hot flashes and night sweats are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have a few mild ones, while others have many times a day, enough to interfere with work or sleep. Some people settle within a few years, others last longer. **What can make them more likely.** People often notice a connection with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress, heavy bedding, etc. These triggers differ greatly between people, so recording your own tags can be more useful than a general list. **There can be other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid disease, infection, some medications, anxiety, and other illnesses. If symptoms don't fit your usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever, or feeling unwell, tell your doctor. **To communicate well.** Information useful at the visit: - Roughly how many times per day and per night - How strong they feel and how long they last - What they get in the way of: sleep, work, conversation, exercise - What seemed to come before - What you have tried so far and whether anything changed. MenoMap's hot flash button and the log-later feature are made precisely so you can keep this information without effort. **Help is available.** There are treatments with hormones and without hormones, and also everyday tips. Which suits you is something to decide in consultation with your doctor.

backTranslations.291: Hormone replacement therapy (often called HRT or MHT) is a treatment that supplements part of the estrogen that decreases in the body around menopause. Major clinical guidelines consider it an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can help with other symptoms too. **There are various forms:** patches, gels, sprays, oral medicine, and low-dose vaginal products used for local symptoms such as dryness. For people who have a uterus, a progestogen is usually prescribed together with the estrogen to protect the uterine lining. **Benefits and risks differ by person:** they depend on age, time since periods stopped, the person's and family's medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, heart disease), and the type and method of treatment. So it is something to decide together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide. **Common questions:** - Is HRT an option for me? Why? - Which type and form do you think is good? Why? - What effects can be expected, and how soon? - What are my personal risks? How do they compare with not treating? - What should I watch for? When should we review? **If you are already using it,** record it in MenoMap (Me -> Medications). MenoMap shows your hot flashes before and after starting as a coincidence check, not proof of cause, so it becomes concrete material to discuss at the review. MenoMap will never recommend starting, stopping, or changing a medication.
backTranslations.292: Hormone replacement therapy is something to decide together with your doctor
backTranslations.293: Hormone replacement therapy is not right for everyone, and some people prefer other approaches. There are several options. **Prescription options.** Among non-hormonal medicines, some have evidence for reducing hot flashes: some medicines originally developed for other illnesses, and a newer type of medicine developed specifically for hot flashes. Each has effects, side effects and interactions, so you can compare and think about them together with your doctor. **Talking and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it lessens the distress of hot flashes and night sweats and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis is also being researched. **Everyday tips many people find helpful:** - Layers that come off quickly - A fan at the desk and bedside - A cool bedroom and breathable bedding - Noticing and easing your own triggers (MenoMap tags and experiments help) - Regular exercise and regular sleep habits. **Supplements and herbal products.** For many the evidence is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medicines. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you use, including over-the-counter products. **Try only one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares your own records before adding a change and while adding it. It is clearer than judging by feel.

backTranslations.403: MenoMap is a tool for wellness records and health education. It does not diagnose menopause or other illnesses, does not prescribe or change treatment, and does not replace care from a qualified doctor. If you are worried about symptoms, or have bleeding after menopause, chest pain, sudden severe headache, weakness on one side of the body, difficulty breathing, or fainting, get in-person care or emergency medical care.
backTranslations.416: Visits are usually short, and it is hard to recall a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the last few days or the worst day. A simple record fills that gap. **What the record tells your doctor:** - Not only whether you have the symptom but how often and how strongly it occurs - Whether it is getting better, worse, or unchanged - What was going on around it: sleep, alcohol, stress, medication - A starting point to compare against if you try a treatment. **Keep it easy.** A record is useful when kept up. MenoMap is built around a one-tap hot flash button and a four-question evening review, so it takes a few seconds without opening a notebook. **Start with two weeks.** With 2 to 4 weeks of records you can usually see a clearer overall picture than from a record of just one hard week. **Bring questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom bothering you most, what you want to try or avoid, worries. In MenoMap's Visit tab, you can pick questions and print them together with the notes.

backTranslations.479: After 12 months have passed with no periods, **any vaginal bleeding needs to be seen by a doctor**. This is the same even if it is only once, even if it is a small spotting or a light pink or brown discharge. In most cases the cause is not serious. For example, thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common. However, bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of an illness that is much easier to treat if found early. So guidance from public health bodies recommends getting it checked rather than waiting and watching. **If you are on hormone replacement therapy,** depending on the type you use, there are somewhat expected bleeding patterns. Bleeding not expected from the treatment, heavier than usual, or off-schedule also needs to be checked. **What to do:** - Contact your doctor or a medical facility and tell them you had bleeding after menopause. - Write down the date, amount, and anything else you notice. You can record it in MenoMap (Me -> Cycle). MenoMap cannot tell why the bleeding happened. It notifies you to get checked, and includes it in the visit notes.

backTranslations.529: Sleep trouble is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and rarely has only one cause. **Night sweats** can wake you by themselves, or heat and dampness can keep you from falling asleep. **Other common factors:** - Needing to go to the toilet at night - Anxiety, or a racing mind - Alcohol (though it may help you fall asleep, it makes sleep in the second half of the night easily broken) - Late caffeine - Pain, restless legs, a partner's snoring - Snoring and pauses in breathing (can be a sign of sleep apnea syndrome; worth discussing, especially if very sleepy in the daytime). **Tips that often help.** A cool dark room, breathable bedding and layers that come off quickly, the same wake time every day, cutting back on alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a well-researched, structured method, and many doctors can guide you to it. **What is good to record.** For 1 to 2 weeks, record sleep score, night hot flashes, alcohol, and late caffeine. With MenoMap's evening review and hot flash log, it is just a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show Health's sleep and wrist skin temperature alongside night sweats. This is not an explanation, it is for reference. **When to see a doctor.** If lack of sleep affects safety (for example driving), mood, or daily life, or if you notice that you stop breathing or gasp at night, talk to a doctor.

verdict: Pass. All safety strings match the English meaning. Every bleeding string uses 閉経後 (after menopause, i.e. after the final period), never 更年期 alone; 479 explicitly defines it as 12 months without a period and keeps 'even once', 'even spotting/light pink or brown discharge', and the HRT-unexpected-bleeding clause. 'Seek care now' (278), the emergency lists (403), 'MenoMap cannot assess/tell why', no start/stop/change medicine advice, and 'coincidence check, not proof of cause' are all preserved. No fixes needed.
